cards.front: What three escape tools does every driver have in an emergency
cards.back: Emergencies find every driver, so preparation and crash prevention are universal duties with three escape tools: braking, steering, and accelerating.

cards.front: How do you brake in an emergency with anti-lock brakes
cards.back: Stopping is the first crash-avoidance instinct, and most new cars carry anti-lock brakes that halt without skidding while preserving steering, so learn your owner's manual, then stomp and hold through normal vibration and clicks while still steering.

cards.front: What do cars without anti-lock brakes follow in an emergency stop
cards.back: Cars without anti-lock brakes follow the owner's manual braking procedure instead.

cards.front: What are the steps of an emergency swerve
cards.back: Swerving around trouble starts with a two-hand grip, aims where you want to go while dodging traffic, then counter-steers straight to regain control and slow down.

cards.front: Where do your hands stay and how do you handle obstacles and darting animals
cards.back: Keep both hands on the wheel except for brief driving tasks, and pair braking with steering against roadway obstacles, braking and steering to miss animals that dart out.

cards.front: When is speeding up the right escape
cards.back: Sometimes the escape is speed, as when another vehicle threatens from behind or the side.

cards.front: How do anti-lock and plain cars differ in emergency braking
cards.back: Anti-lock cars stomp and hold through clicks and shudders, while non-anti-lock cars follow the owner's manual instead.

cards.front: How do swerves and animal encounters differ in response
cards.back: Swerves steer around and counter-steer straight, while animal encounters brake and steer together.

cards.front: Which escape fits threats ahead and which fits threats from behind or the side
cards.back: Braking and steering dodge threats ahead, while accelerating dodges strikes from behind or the side.

cards.front: What causes skids and what makes them worse
cards.back: Skids strike from excess speed, panic stops, or lost grip and leave little control, while panicking, brake-stomping, and overcorrecting only deepen the skid toward a fatal crash.

cards.front: What do you do first in a skid and how do you slow an anti-lock car
cards.back: Skidding, release both pedals and stare where you want to go, adding steady brake pressure to slow a straight-line slide in an anti-lock car.

cards.front: How do you slow a skidding car without anti-lock brakes
cards.back: Without anti-lock brakes, never brake hard since locked wheels worsen skids; slow the car with gentle brake pumps instead.

cards.front: How do you recover from a sideways skid
cards.back: In a sideways skid, steer toward the sliding rear to realign the nose, then unwind promptly as the car straightens to block a counter-skid.

cards.front: How long do you keep correcting and which control matters most in a skid
cards.back: Keep seesawing the wheel until the skid fully releases, since the steering wheel outranks every other skid control.

cards.front: What do you do when your wheels drop off the pavement edge
cards.back: Off the pavement edge, refuse panic yanks back up; slow gradually and, when safe, turn briskly back on.
cards.memory_hook: No yank, slow, turn back briskly

cards.front: How do anti-lock and plain cars differ in a skid
cards.back: Anti-lock skids take steady brake pressure, while plain skids take gentle pumps and never a stomp.

cards.front: What is the sequence for a sideways skid
cards.back: Sideways skids steer into the sliding rear, then unwind fast to block the counter-skid.

cards.front: What must you do after any collision and where do non-injury wrecks go
cards.back: After any collision, stop at or near the scene, stay until the officer finishes questioning, and under Kentucky law shift non-injury wrecks to the shoulder per KRS one hundred eighty-nine point five eight zero, subsection one, paragraph b.

cards.front: What information do you log after a crash
cards.back: Log every operator's name, address, and license number, each car's plate, VIN, make, model, and year, each insurer's name and phone, a damage list with photos, and exactly what happened just before and after impact.

cards.front: What do you do after striking a parked car
cards.back: For parked-car strikes, hunt the owner or leave a visible note bearing your name, address, license and plate numbers, plus the date and time.

cards.front: When must you file a written crash report and by when
cards.back: Property damage over five hundred dollars without a police investigation demands a written report to the Kentucky State Police within ten days of the crash.

cards.front: How do you aid the injured and when may you move them
cards.back: Aid the injured with prompt proper care, summon medics and troopers with a precise location, move victims only to save a life, otherwise await the ambulance while blanketing them warm.
cards.memory_hook: Aid, summon, move only to save

cards.front: What does Kentucky law order every involved operator to do
cards.back: Kentucky law orders every involved operator to stop at once, size up injuries and damage, and render reasonable aid including carrying or arranging transport for treatment when plainly needed or requested.

cards.front: How do injury scenes and non-injury wrecks differ in what you do
cards.back: Injury scenes hold position until questioned, while non-injury wrecks shift to the shoulder.

cards.front: How does a driver-to-driver crash differ from a parked-car strike in what you record
cards.back: Driver-to-driver crashes log full identities and damage, while parked-car strikes leave a dated note.

cards.front: How is a collision report filed and when is it skipped
cards.back: Collision reports e-file through the portal or mail to Frankfort, but never when an officer investigated.
cards.memory_hook: Portal or mail, skip if officer

cards.front: When may crash victims be moved
cards.back: Victims move only to save a life, otherwise awaiting the ambulance under blankets.

cards.front: How do you head off vehicle failures and what warning must never be ignored
cards.back: Honor the owner's manual service schedule to head off failures, watch warning lamps, and never drive under a brake warning.

cards.front: What do you do when the brakes fail while rolling
cards.back: Brakeless while rolling, drag the parking brake slowly against rear-wheel lockup and skid, poised to release if the tail steps out.

cards.front: What if the parking brake fails too
cards.back: If the parking brake fails too, kill the engine, coast to a safe off-road stop, and never drive on without working brakes.

cards.front: How does a car behave in a front blowout versus a rear blowout
cards.back: Blowouts vent tires instantly, yanking front-tire cars hard toward the burst side while rear-tire cars wobble, shake, and drift that way.

cards.front: What do you do during a blowout
cards.back: On a blowout, clamp the wheel straight, lift off the gas, and shun the brake, letting the car coast down or braking only feather-light.
cards.memory_hook: Clamp wheel, off gas, no brake

cards.front: Where do you stop after a blowout and what do you do there
cards.back: Never halt on the roadway when avoidable; limp to a safe shoulder, flash the hazards, and fit a fresh tire.

cards.front: What do you do when the engine dies while rolling
cards.back: Dead engine rolling, muscle the heavy-but-turnable wheel, pick an escape path, and brake steadily rather than hard while easing off the road.

cards.front: What do you do once a dead-engine car has halted
cards.back: Halted, retry the starter, and on failure raise the hood, light the flashers, and call for help.

cards.front: What do you do about a runaway accelerator
cards.back: For a runaway accelerator, switch the engine off, grab neutral, find an escape path, steer smooth, brake soft, pull clear, and fix the pedal before driving again.

cards.front: Where do you park a broken-down car
cards.back: Breakdowns kill visibility, so park fully off to the right when possible or where distant drivers can spot you, never just past a crest or bend, flashing hazards with the hood raised.
cards.memory_hook: Fully off right, never past crest

cards.front: Where do you place warning flares and whom do you call
cards.back: Plant warning flares two hundred to three hundred feet behind the disabled car to buy lane-change time, and phone authorities, whose numbers many roadways post.
cards.memory_hook: Flares two to three hundred back

cards.front: In what order do you respond to dead brakes
cards.back: Dead brakes try the parking brake first, then the engine switch as the last resort.

cards.front: How do front and rear blowouts differ
cards.back: Front blowouts yank toward the burst side, while rear blowouts wobble, shake, and drift.

cards.front: How do power failures and runaway accelerators differ in first response
cards.back: Power failures brake steadily to the shoulder, while runaway accelerators switch off and grab neutral first.

cards.front: Where should breakdowns never park and where do flares go
cards.back: Breakdowns shun crests and bends for parking, then plant flares two hundred to three hundred feet behind.

recap_hooks.text: Brake, steer, or accelerate; stomp anti-lock, counter-steer swerves
Release pedals, look where going, steer into the slide
Stop and stay, log everything, report in ten days, aid the hurt
Parking brake first, clamp on blowouts, engine off for runaways, flares far back

merges.justification: The accepted statement of sec09-F17 contains the slash symbol inside the web address "https://kspportal.ky.gov slash CivilianCollisionReporting", which the spoken-form back check rejects and which must not be altered; its report-filing content (portal or mail to Frankfort, no form when an officer investigated) is carried by the sibling card sec09-R08 in the same module (the fact keeps its KG node, exam item and lesson citations).
